**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The narrative blurb recounts that the Buddha related this past-life story while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with a lay gardener in Sāvatthī. Serving a local squire who was hosting the Buddha and the monastic community, the gardener displayed an extraordinary skill: simply by glancing up at a tree from the ground, he could accurately determine whether its fruit was unripe, nearly ripe, or fully ripe. When the monks marveled at his expertise, the Buddha declared that wise persons of antiquity possessed an identical knowledge of fruits, prompting the narration of the past tale.

In the epigraphic labels of the medieval temples at Pagan, the title of the narrative shows minor regional variations: the temple of Gubyaukgyi (Wetkyi-in) identifies it as *Kimphala*, whereas the Ānanda temple labels it *Phalaka*, and other local temples use the form *Phala* [WinThanTun 2002].
